##### Upper Critical Values of the F Distribution {#sec-eda-f-distribution-table}

This table contains the upper critical values of the [F distribution](#sec-eda-f-distribution). This table is used for one-sided F tests at the $\alpha$ = 0.05, 0.10, and 0.01 levels.

More specifically, a test statistic is computed with $\nu_1$ and $\nu_2$ degrees of freedom, and the result is compared to this table. For a one-sided test, the null hypothesis is rejected when the test statistic is greater than the tabled value. This is demonstrated with the graph of an F distribution with $\nu_1 = 10$ and $\nu_2 = 10$. The shaded area of the graph indicates the rejection region at the $\alpha$ significance level. Since this is a one-sided test, we have $\alpha$ probability in the upper tail of exceeding the critical value and zero in the lower tail. Because the F distribution is asymmetric, a two-sided test requires a set of tables (not included here) that contain the rejection regions for both the lower and upper tails.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-f-distribution-table-shaded
#| fig-cap: "One-sided test for alpha = 0.05 (F distribution, 10 and 10 df)"
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)

df1 <- 10
df2 <- 10
crit <- qf(0.95, df1, df2)

tibble(x = seq(0.001, 5, length.out = 401)) |>
  mutate(y = df(x, df1, df2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = ~ filter(.x, x >= crit),
    aes(ymin = 0, ymax = y),
    fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

Given a specified value of $\alpha$, find the column corresponding to $\nu_1$ and the row corresponding to $\nu_2$ and reject the null hypothesis if the test statistic is greater than the tabled value.

The following tables for $\nu_2$ from 1 to 100 and $\nu_1$ from 1 to 20 are included. (The original handbook split each of these into two tables, for $\nu_1$ = 1–10 and 11–20, purely to fit 1990s page widths; they are combined into a single table here.)

**5% significance level** — $F_{.05}(\nu_1, \nu_2)$

::: {style="overflow-x: auto;"}
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: tbl-f-distribution-05
crossing(nu2 = 1:100, nu1 = 1:20) |>
  mutate(f = qf(0.95, nu1, nu2)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = nu1, values_from = f, names_prefix = "v") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("nu2", as.character(1:20)))
```
:::

**10% significance level** — $F_{.10}(\nu_1, \nu_2)$

::: {style="overflow-x: auto;"}
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: tbl-f-distribution-10
crossing(nu2 = 1:100, nu1 = 1:20) |>
  mutate(f = qf(0.90, nu1, nu2)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = nu1, values_from = f, names_prefix = "v") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("nu2", as.character(1:20)))
```
:::

**1% significance level** — $F_{.01}(\nu_1, \nu_2)$

::: {style="overflow-x: auto;"}
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: tbl-f-distribution-01
crossing(nu2 = 1:100, nu1 = 1:20) |>
  mutate(f = qf(0.99, nu1, nu2)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = nu1, values_from = f, names_prefix = "v") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("nu2", as.character(1:20)))
```
:::
